concepts.why: Academic scholar / Jewish reader: Deuteronomy 29:9 is the covenant made in the land of Moab (29:1 calls it 'in addition to the covenant He had made with them at Horeb'), not the covenant at Sinai/Horeb; the name says Sinai, so the verse does not hold it. Every other passage is Sinai/Horeb and every note is an exact quotation.

Academic / Jewish reader: Leviticus 19:34 says to love the foreigner 'as yourself'; it does not say 'neighbor', and 19:18 and 19:34 use different words in the Hebrew. Placing it here makes the site say the foreigner is the neighbor. It already stands in concept 10, where it belongs; the six quotations of 19:18 that remain are all of that phrase.

concepts.name: The essence of the Law and the Prophets
concepts.why: Biblical-theological and academic readers: the name (Matthew 22:40) says the Law and the Prophets hang on these TWO commandments. Matthew 7:12 (the rule of doing to others), Romans 13:8 and 13:10 (love of neighbor only) and Mark 12:33 (love above sacrifices) do not speak of the two. 'Essence' is Matthew 7:12's own word, 'summed up/fulfillment' is Romans 13's, and Matthew 22:40 and Mark 12:31 stay in as quotations under it, so no passage says less than the name. Overlap with concepts 4 and 5 is welcome and kept.

concepts.name: Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy
concepts.why: Seventh-day / Reformed (Lord's Day) / dispensational / Lutheran / Orthodox readers part on the Sabbath, and as drafted the concept holds only the Sabbath commanded (Exodus, Deuteronomy, Isaiah) and Jesus as 'Lord even of the Sabbath', and none of the New Testament texts that treat the day as a matter of conscience or as a shadow. Hiding them would lean one way. Add, each with an exact note: Romans 14:5 ('One person regards one day above another, while another regards every day alike'), Colossians 2:16-17 (quote 2:16 only: 'let no one judge you ... with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath') and Hebrews 4:9 ('There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God'); no concept name or note may say which reading is right. The name is brought to Exodus 20:8's exact words (BSB), since 'Keep the Sabbath day holy' is a reordered quotation that reads as the site's own command.

concepts.name: Your law is my delight
concepts.why: Academic / Jewish reader: 'My delight is in Your law' is not any verse's wording (Psalm 119:77 is 'Your law is my delight'; Psalm 1:2 is 'his delight is in the Law of the LORD'), so the name is renamed to Psalm 119:77's exact words. Joshua 1:8 commands meditation for success and says nothing of delight, so it shares a word with the concept (it fits concept 11 or 16 better, or is simply dropped). Move in Psalm 37:31 from concept 24 ('The law of his God is in his heart'), which says the same as Psalm 40:8 and does not promise a new heart.

Biblical-theological and Reformed/Lutheran/Catholic readers: James 2:10 is about the whole law broken at one point, not about being doers of the word; it belongs with Deuteronomy 27:26 and Galatians 3:10 in concept 13 ('Cursed is he who does not ... continue to do everything written'). Left here it reads as the site's gloss on James 1:22.

concepts.name: Christ and the law
concepts.why: Lutheran, Reformed, Catholic, Orthodox, Wesleyan, dispensational and Jewish readers all part here. The exact quotation 'I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them' is Matthew 5:17 only, yet it heads a group that includes Romans 10:4 ('Christ is the end of the law'), Galatians 3:24 (guardian) and Romans 3:31 (uphold). Under that heading the site appears to answer in 'not abolish' the very question Romans 10:4 raises, so the dispensational and Lutheran readers would object, and a Jewish or academic reader would see Paul's 'end' (telos, which translations render 'end' and 'goal/culmination') forced under Jesus's sentence. Do not drop any passage: dropping Romans 10:4 would hide an obvious link. The plain label 'Christ and the law' holds every passage, takes no side, and Matthew 5:17 is still shown in full with its exact-quotation note. On Romans 10:4, the original (telos) arbitrates, so its note should stay the exact words 'Christ is the end of the law' with no gloss and the site should not choose between 'end' and 'goal'.

concepts.name: The law and sin
concepts.why: Academic and Jewish readers: the name states in the site's voice, as a flat claim, one of Paul's sentences ('the law merely brings awareness of sin'), and four of the seven passages say something else: Romans 4:15 (wrath, no transgression), 5:13 (sin not taken into account), 5:20 (trespass would increase), Galatians 3:19 (added because of transgressions). The name says less than the passages say. The plain label 'The law and sin' (Romans 7:7: 'Is the law sin? Certainly not!') holds all seven with their exact notes and does not present Paul's account as what the Torah itself claims to do.

note_fixes: James 2:21-24 (replacing the two cuts): keep the note 'Was not our father Abraham justified by what he did' on 2:21 and 'a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone' on 2:24, but give the passage as 2:21-24 whole
concepts.why: Lutheran, Reformed, Catholic, Wesleyan readers: James is cut at 2:21-22 and 2:24, leaving out 2:23, the verse that quotes 'Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness'. That is the sentence Paul quotes, so skipping it turns the pairing into a bare contradiction that the texts themselves do not state and makes James look like the only voice on works. Give James 2:21-24 whole. Also add Romans 4:2-3 with the same quotation (note: 'Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness') so that both writers' use of Abraham appears; the site still does not reconcile them. 'Each in its own words' is otherwise the right handling; the other notes are exact.

concepts.name: Under the law
concepts.why: Reformed, Catholic, Orthodox, Wesleyan and Jewish readers: 'Not under law, but under grace' is Romans 6:14, and the other passages do not say it: 1 Corinthians 9:20-21 (Paul as under, and not under, the law, and 'under the law of Christ'), Galatians 3:23-25 (held in custody under the law), Galatians 4:4-5 (Christ himself 'born under the law'), Romans 7:6 (released). Only one carries 'under grace'. As a heading in the site's voice it states the dispensational and Lutheran reading as the group's content, while Reformed, Catholic and Orthodox readers take 'under law' as under its condemnation, not its commands. 'Under the law' is the one phrase every passage uses, and Romans 6:14-15 (with its 'Certainly not!') stays in full with its note.

concepts.name: Wisdom and the commandments
concepts.why: Biblical-theological and academic readers: the name is Psalm 111:10, but Deuteronomy 4:5-6 (the law shows wisdom), Deuteronomy 10:12-13 (fear and keep the commandments, no word of wisdom), Psalm 19:7 and 119:98-100 (the law makes wise) do not say that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; only Psalm 111:10 and, by implication, Ecclesiastes 12:13 do. 'The one bridge to wisdom' is better named by a plain label. Ps 111:10 stays and keeps its full note.

The last concept is the theme's own words of hope, and it is: every remaining passage is a promise that God will do something to the heart (Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 31:33-34; Ezekiel 11:19-20, 36:26-27; Hebrews 8:10 quoting Jeremiah; 2 Corinthians 3:3), all in the texts' words, nothing interpretive in the name or the notes, and no note needs fixing. Nothing dark was left out to make room: the curse, the letter that kills, the law's weakness and the 'under a curse' texts all stand elsewhere. But two passages do not promise a new heart: Psalm 37:31 (a present description of the righteous) and Deuteronomy 30:11-14 (the commandment is near). Neither says 'I will give you'. Move Psalm 37:31 to concept 15 beside Psalm 40:8, and Deuteronomy 30:11-14 to concept 12 (the same chapter as 30:19). All traditions can read this, including the dispensational reader (to whom Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 are promises to Israel) and the Reformed/Catholic readers (to whom Hebrews 8 and 2 Corinthians 3 take them up), because the name and notes say neither.

secondary_or_links: Order: 17 ('You have heard that it was said', Matthew 5:21-44) comes before 18 (Matthew 5:17-19 etc.), the reverse of Matthew's own order; putting 18 first follows the text and does not suggest the sayings are the answer to 5:17. Low risk either way; recommended.

Concepts 12 and 24: consider adding Romans 10:6-8 (note: 'The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart') after Romans 10:5. It quotes Deuteronomy 30:12-14 and shows the New Testament citing the same chapter that gives 'Choose life'; cutting Romans 10:5 off from its next verse leaves the contrast Paul draws out of view. Also optional in 12: Galatians 3:12 and Nehemiah 9:29, the other places that quote or echo Leviticus 18:5.
Concept 13: James 2:10 may be added here (moved from concept 16).

Secondary 'Law -> Certificate of divorce' and 'Law -> Eye for eye': fine as table rows; the notes are exact quotations. Optional secondary additions where the texts pair a commandment with Jesus's own use of it: 'Honor your father and mother' (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16; Matthew 15:4-6; Ephesians 6:2) and 'Mercy, not sacrifice' (Hosea 6:6; Matthew 9:13; Matthew 12:7).

Links: Ten themes are fine. 'Priesthood' was dropped on the ground that no passage truly overlaps, but Exodus 19:6 ('a kingdom of priests') and Malachi 2:7 (the priest's lips preserve knowledge) are in this outline, so if the theme exists, restore it. If themes called Justice / Faith / Israel exist, they would be natural links from concepts 9 and 20; otherwise leave.

missing.sub_theme: All Israel has transgressed Your law
missing.why: Biblical-theological and Jewish readers: the texts plainly develop how the law was broken and the curse of Deuteronomy 28 and 29 fell ('the curse and sworn judgment written in the Law of Moses', Daniel 9:11). The outline moves from the curse (13) through praise (14, 15) to the promise (24) without this link, which is exactly what the hope in 24 answers. It is the dark counterpart to the closing concept and belongs before it.

missing.sub_theme: The Gentiles and the law of Moses
missing.why: All nine readers expect the Jerusalem council in a theme about the law and the New Testament, and Acts 15:10 ('a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear') is the New Testament's one heavy statement of the law as a burden, set against the 'not burdensome' (1 John 5:3) and 'delight' of 14 and 15. Romans 2:14-15 (those who do not have the law, 'the work of the law written on their hearts') is the other plain text. No note may say which tradition's reading of the council is right.

Dispensational, Lutheran and academic readers: the outline holds 'I have not come to abolish' (Matthew 5:17), 'uphold the law' (Romans 3:31) and Luke 16:17, but not the verses that say 'change of law', 'obsolete', 'abolishing in His flesh the law of commandments and ordinances' and the record 'canceled'. Leaving out the clearest texts on one pole while keeping the other leans toward continuity; the site's two renamed concepts (18, 21) stay neutral, but only the full set of texts is. 'A change of law' is Hebrews 7:12's wording ('there must also be a change of law').

Jewish, Reformed and Catholic readers: Jesus names 'the more important matters of the law -- justice, mercy, and faithfulness' (BSB: 'justice and mercy and faithfulness'), linking directly to Micah 6:8 in concept 9, and twice quotes 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice' from Hosea. Mark 12:33 in concept 6 is the only trace of this theme; it deserves its own concept in the texts' words.

missing.sub_theme: Is the law opposed to the promises of God?
missing.why: Lutheran, Reformed, dispensational and Jewish readers: the texts explicitly ask how the law stands to the promise made to Abraham four hundred and thirty years earlier ('Is the law, then, opposed to the promises of God? Certainly not!'). Concepts 1, 19 and 20 touch the verses around it (Galatians 3:19; Romans 4:15) but the question the texts themselves ask is not shown. Give it in the verses' own words with no note saying how it is answered beyond what the verse says.
